21.event_title: Francis of Assisi renounces his inheritance
21.event: In early 1206 Francis's father, the wealthy cloth merchant Pietro di Bernardone, brought him before the bishop of Assisi and demanded that he renounce all claims and return his goods. Francis gave up his inheritance and handed back even the clothes he wore, and the bishop covered him with his own cloak. Francis went on to live in poverty and founded the Franciscan order, which has honoured him ever since.
21.explanation: Francis's public act of letting go of wealth became one of the most celebrated renunciations in European history, and he is still revered across the world eight centuries later.
21.tie_back: The kural says the settled verdict of all good books is to praise those who have let go of desire, and Francis's renunciation is among the most praised such acts in the Christian tradition.
21._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of a renunciant honoured above worldly excellence, though the kural's point about textual consensus is not shown by a single event.

22.event_title: Mother Teresa receives the Nobel Peace Prize
22.event: Mother Teresa, who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta (Kolkata), India, in 1950 after taking religious vows, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1979. The Norwegian Nobel Committee cited her work for bringing help to suffering humanity. She received the prize in Oslo in December 1979.
22.explanation: The world's most prominent peace award was given to a nun who owned almost nothing, recognising a kind of greatness that cannot be measured in wealth or power.
22.tie_back: The kural says measuring the greatness of renunciants is like counting all the dead, and the Nobel honour for a woman who had given up everything shows the world struggling to put a measure on such greatness.
22._accuracy_note: The prize honours a renunciant's greatness, but the kural's point that such greatness is beyond counting cannot be shown directly by any event.

23.event_title: Emperor Charles V abdicates and retires to the monastery of Yuste
23.event: In Brussels on 25 October 1555, Charles V, ruler of the Holy Roman Empire, Spain and the Netherlands, began giving up his realms, handing the Netherlands and Spain to his son Philip and the imperial title to his brother Ferdinand. He sailed to Spain in 1556 and in February 1557 moved to the monastery of Yuste. He lived there in relative seclusion until his death on 21 September 1558.
23.explanation: The most powerful monarch in Europe chose to lay down his crowns while still alive and end his days beside a monastery, an almost unique act among rulers of his age.
23.tie_back: The kural praises those who have weighed this world against the other and taken up the path of virtue here and now, and Charles V, having held more of the world than almost anyone, chose to leave it for a life of retreat.
23._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of discerning the two orders and choosing the spiritual, though the sources do not record his inner reasoning.

24.event_title: Eric Liddell declines to run on Sunday at the Paris Olympics
24.event: When the programme for the 1924 Paris Olympics was issued, the Scottish sprinter Eric Liddell learned that the heats of the 100 metres, his strongest event, would be run on a Sunday. As a devout Christian who would not compete on the Sabbath, he withdrew and trained instead for the 200 and 400 metres. He won bronze in the 200 metres and gold in the 400 metres in an Olympic record time of 47.6 seconds.
24.explanation: Liddell gave up his best chance of glory because of a principle he had settled in advance, and still triumphed in an event that was not his speciality.
24.tie_back: The kural praises the one who controls the five senses with the goad of firm resolve, and Liddell's steady resolve held back the strongest desire an athlete has, the desire to win in his best event.
24._accuracy_note: A good example of firmness of mind overruling desire, though it concerns ambition rather than the five senses.

25.event_title: Emperor Akbar honours the hermit Salim Chishti at Sikri
25.event: In 1568-69 the Mughal emperor Akbar visited the Sufi hermit Shaikh Salim Chishti, who lived on the ridge at Sikri, and Chishti foretold that Akbar would have an heir. Akbar's son Salim, the future emperor Jahangir, was born at Sikri in 1569. Akbar then moved his court there and built Fatehpur Sikri, whose Jama Masjid, completed in 1571-72, came to enclose the saint's tomb.
25.explanation: One of the most powerful emperors in the world built an entire capital beside a hermit's dwelling, a striking public acknowledgement of an ascetic's standing.
25.tie_back: The kural says Indra, king of the heavens, is witness to the power of one who has quenched the senses, and here an earthly emperor bore that witness by building his capital in honour of a hermit.
25._accuracy_note: A strong parallel of a sovereign testifying to an ascetic's power, with an emperor standing in for the kural's Indra.

26.event_title: Hillary and Tenzing make the first ascent of Everest
26.event: On 29 May 1953 Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa mountaineer, reached the summit of Mount Everest, becoming the first people known to stand on the world's highest mountain. Tenzing had taken part in six earlier attempts on the mountain going back to 1935. The two men spent about fifteen minutes on top before descending.
26.explanation: After decades of failed attempts, the climb became a worldwide symbol of doing what had seemed impossible.
26.tie_back: The kural defines the great as those who do what is hard to do, and the first ascent of Everest is one of history's clearest cases of people achieving what others could not.
26._accuracy_note: A clear fit for the kural's test of greatness, though the kural is in a chapter on ascetics and Everest is a physical rather than moral feat.

27.event_title: Helen Keller understands the word water
27.event: Helen Keller, who had lost her sight and hearing in early childhood, began lessons with her teacher Anne Sullivan in March 1887. On 5 April 1887 Sullivan held Helen's hand under a water pump and spelled w-a-t-e-r into her other hand, and Helen suddenly understood that the finger signs named the water. By that evening she had learned some thirty words, and she went on to become a writer and lecturer.
27.explanation: With two senses closed to her, Keller gained her hold on the whole world by understanding deeply what touch could tell her.
27.tie_back: The kural says the world is in the grasp of one who truly discerns the nature of the senses, and Keller's breakthrough came when she grasped what a single sense could carry.
27._accuracy_note: A vivid case of understanding the senses opening up the world, though the kural concerns an ascetic's discernment rather than learning language.

28.event_title: The Diamond Sutra, the world's earliest dated printed book
28.event: A Chinese copy of the Diamond Sutra, a Buddhist scripture, was printed from carved wooden blocks and dated by its colophon to the equivalent of 11 May 868. It was found in the early 20th century among tens of thousands of scrolls in a sealed cave at the Mogao Buddhist cave site near Dunhuang. It is the earliest dated complete printed book known and is now held by the British Library.
28.explanation: The words of a teacher of renunciation were thought important enough to become the subject of the first dated printed book, and they have survived more than eleven centuries.
28.tie_back: The kural says the greatness of those whose words are full of power is shown by the sacred sayings they leave behind, and the Diamond Sutra is a striking case of such sayings being preserved and spread.
28._accuracy_note: A good fit for sacred sayings that outlast their speaker, though the printing shows devotion to the words rather than proving their power.

29.event: The celebrated novelist Emile Zola published an open letter to the President of France, Felix Faure, in the newspaper L'Aurore, defending Captain Alfred Dreyfus and accusing the army of covering up his wrongful conviction for treason. About 200,000 copies were sold that day, and the letter became the turning point of the Dreyfus affair. Zola was convicted of libel, but the case was reopened and Dreyfus was fully cleared in 1906.
29.explanation: The public anger of a respected figure turned a buried injustice into a national cause that the guilty could no longer hide.
29.tie_back: The kural warns that when those of high character are roused to anger the offender cannot be shielded, and Zola's letter stripped away the protection around those who had wronged Dreyfus.
29._accuracy_note: Zola was not an ascetic and the wrongdoers were exposed over years, not in an instant, so the fit is partial.

30.event_title: Albert Schweitzer and Reverence for Life
30.event: Albert Schweitzer, a theologian, musician and doctor, went in 1913 to Lambarene on the Ogooue River in what is now Gabon, where he and his wife Helene built a hospital. In 1915, while travelling on the river, the phrase Reverence for Life came to him, and it became the centre of his ethics, extending moral concern to every living thing. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952, cited for his altruism, reverence for life and tireless humanitarian work.
30.explanation: Schweitzer turned a principle of compassion toward all life into decades of practical service, and the world honoured him for it.
30.tie_back: The kural says the truly virtuous are those who wear unbroken compassion toward every living being, and Schweitzer's Reverence for Life is almost a restatement of that standard in modern form.
30._accuracy_note: Nearly a dramatisation of the kural: compassion toward all life as the mark of the truly virtuous.
